newsitem.title: CHILE: Chile's Enami mulls refinery transfer to Codelco.
newsitem.headline: Chile's Enami mulls refinery transfer to Codelco.

text.p: A Chilean government commission has recommended transferring state copper company Enami's Ventanas smelting and refining complex to state copper giant Codelco's Andina division, newspaper El Mercurio reported.

The transfer is logical because the Ventanas plant already buys large amounts of concentrates from the nearby Andina mine for processing, said Empresa Nacional de Mineria (Enami) vice president Claudio Agostini in an interview.
"With this scheme we could maximise the profits of this group of companies," said Agostini.
Ventanas would become a new subsidiary of Codelco but would also include workers and private pension funds among its shareholders, he said.
The plan -- still in its early stages -- is part of a government drive to slim down Enami whose main purpose is to help small, private mining companies.
Enami buys concentrates from these mines at prices that allow them to operate economically, leading critics to call it essentially a state subsidy for pits which would otherwise go under.
The report proposes that these small firms finance the building of a refinery at Enami's Paipote smelter as their production will no longer be processed at Ventanas.
The refinery at Ventanas, which lies on the Pacific coast north of Santiago, would in future only process concentrates from Andina and anodes from Codelco's El Teniente division.
Paipote processes 260,000 tonnes of concentrates a year, while the recently-expanded Ventanas plant has a production capacity of 330,000 tonnes of copper a year.
Enami will in future concentrate its efforts on helping only the smallest copper mines, said Agostini.
"Considering Chile's economic level and the mining sector in particular, the role of Enami should be focussed on encouraging small mining companies and not medium-sized ones," he said.
The commission's study is a revision of an earlier report which recommended selling Ventanas and Paipote to private companies.
The first study, leaked to the media two months ago, sparked a furious reaction from state copper mining unions who threatened a national strike.
